title: Modernizing Medical Standards for Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Cases
pass_4_primary_concern: The broad AME pathway is not matched by equally specific treatment-level safeguards, alternatives analysis, and outcome monitoring.
pass_5_high_stakes_domain_reason: The proposal changes medical certification screening for people exercising aviation privileges.
pass_5_red_flag_gates: Harm Before Review Plus Structural Lever
pass_5_concise_why: The proposal is coherent and potentially beneficial, but its broad implementation depends on unspecified safeguards and monitoring in a safety-sensitive domain.
pass_5_most_important_consequence: A weakly specified AME pathway could create inconsistent decisions or delay detection of adverse safety signals.

comments_clusters.representative_excerpt: I fully support the proposed change to eliminate the requirement for a special issuance for non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus. An airman who successfully uses non insulin medications should not have to be required to complete a recertification every year by completing costly testing and doctor visits. I also agree the government will save money not...

A second issue concerns how NIDDM cases will be screened going forward. Once diabetes mellitus controlled by non-insulin medication is no longer independently disqualifying, an NIDDM applicant's case will be evaluated by an Aviation Medical Examiner under the general medical standards, with the AME retaining discretion to defer a higher-risk case to FAA....

I raise it because it illustrates the point the NPRM makes: routing well-controlled, non-insulin cases through Special Issuance creates administrative complexity disproportionate to any safety benefit, and complexity produces mistakes. The information the FAA relies on to certify me — a current A1C, a treating provider's attestation regarding medications...

As a very healthy Type2 pilot, I support the elimination of Type2 (non-insulin treatment) from medical disqualification. Even without a Special Issuance requirement, pilots with Type 2 diabetes remain legally obligated under §61.53 to self-ground whenever symptoms, complications, medication side effects, or glucose abnormalities would make flight unsafe....

B/ Is in the public interest due to FAA cost savings and industrial cost savings. However, the FAA did not calculate similar cost savings relative to removing the blanket ban on “insulin” for ITDM. It is critically important that the FAA expand their conclusions to the ITDM community and strike 14 CFR 67.113(a), 67.213(a), and 67.313(a) in their entirety....

My Doctor put me on Metformin 500mg as a precaution and after telling my AME, i sat thru a 60 day temporary revocation review. Then the FAA said Ok. It does not eliminate medical oversight. Rather, it allows an Aviation Medical Examiner to evaluate an applicant's individual condition, treatment, stability, and medical history while retaining the ability to defer higher-risk cases to the FAA when additional review is warranted. I particularly support reducing unnecessary Special Issuance processing for...

Aviation medical standards should reflect current medical knowledge and actual functional risk. Allowing AMEs to certify pilots whose non-insulin-dependent diabetes is demonstrably well managed accomplishes that while preserving an appropriate pathway for additional FAA review when it is warranted. I encourage the FAA to adopt the proposed change....

As a type 2 diabetic who does not take insulin with a A1C of 5.5 (normal range!) there is no reason for the FAA to require a special issuance. Especially in a case like mine where the same doctor has seen me for over 20 years and there are records showing the A1C every 6 months.

I think this is a marvelous idea. I am an airline pilot with type 2 diabetes. With diet, exercise, and metformin I keep my A1C in the 5's. To be able to go into my AME with current A1C information and get my medical on the spot would be both a benefit to me and a reduction of workload for the FAA.

FAA-2026-10990 — Modernizing Medical Standards for Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Cases As someone who has gone through the special issuance process for this many times I strongly support this change that will reduce the burden without impacting safety.

The burden on everyone is immense and creates undue stress on the system, which would benefit from this change. We trust our AME's to issue our medicals and to no longer classify this as a disqualifying medical condition is the correct solution; the FAA analysis supports making the change. This rule change should become policy as soon as practical.
